subject: soapstoneBear
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: polar bear.
Style: Inuit soapstone carving.
reasoning:
I'm envisioning the carving as a stylized Inuit soapstone polar bear: smooth, chunky, rounded form in dark grey-green stone with polish, incised details, and inlaid eyes, structured with a resting pose and a separate jaw. I want to keep the build manageable in scope while planning out the structure.

For the actual bear, I'm thinking real-ish scale but with chunky stylized proportions -- a big head, thick short legs. The stone surface needs a mottled dark green-grey paint with lighter veins and a polished look, warmer tones on top and cooler underneath. I'm considering incised fur strokes as decal textures applied to the body loft, plus bone-white inlaid eyes, a black nose inlay, and ivory-colored claw inlays, while skipping a base since the brief doesn't call for one.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: a hips root joint near the pelvis, with a spine chain running forward through catmull-rom points up to a chest tip joint, figuring out how many named joints are needed so the spline spans line up correctly with a proper tip name.

Continuing, I'm defining the neck chain extending from the chest to a head base, picking out points so the spans and tip joint align, then attaching the head as its own joint parented to the neck's tip with a slightly downward forward orientation. I'm also setting up a jaw joint parented to the head, positioned using local head coordinates.

For positioning details like ears or decals, I'll use a helper that maps forward/up/left offsets relative to the head's local frame. I'm also adding a short stubby tail chain behind the hips, and planning four thick, mostly-straight legs using a limb structure with two segments plus a paw for each.

Still working out leg attachment and bend details...

Writing paw geometry and leg sweep...

I'm extending the body path slightly past the hips to cover the rump, thinking through how joint ownership clamps affect that trailing segment, and considering whether to just sweep the body using the same path as the spine with an extend option to keep things simple.

Checking the round cap math, the body ends up spanning roughly -1.21 to 0.95, giving a total length near 2.9 with the head included, which runs a bit longer than a real polar bear but works fine for a stylized sculpt.

I'm scaling down the spine heights and leg lengths to keep shoulder height realistic—settling on spine points around y=0.92-1.08 with belly bottom near 0.6 and legs about 0.55 long, plus considering a shoulder hump sphere for that characteristic bear silhouette.

Mapping out radii at different spine points using a profile function to interpolate rx/ry smoothly, with the belly bottom around 0.55-0.58 and shoulders peaking near 1.45-1.5 before adding the hump. Now working out the front leg joint positions for shoulder and wrist.

Checking leg lengths against reach distances to ensure a slight knee bend looks natural for both front and hind legs, then verifying leg radii merge cleanly into the body without poking through. Also figuring out paw placement so they sink slightly into the floor at the correct height.

Writing paw and toe geometry...

Toes land just above the floor plane, good. Now I'm designing the bear head: a rounded skull sphere with a tapered snout, separate upper and lower jaw pieces, small rounded ear discs, a dark inlaid nose at the snout tip, inlaid eyes, an incised mouth line, and brow ridges — positioning the head where the neck meets the chest point.

Working out the neck connecting chest to head, and establishing the head's local coordinate frame relative to its joint so I can place the skull sphere and other features consistently, considering how orientation and scale interact for part placement.

For the snout, I'm sweeping a tapered shape along the head's local axes with tapering radii, giving it round caps, and planning to split the lower jaw into a separate bone-driven piece beneath the upper snout.

I'm checking the overlap between the snout bottom and jaw top to keep the mouth closed convincingly, sizing the lower jaw slimmer than the snout for a soapstone bear look, and considering whether a thin incised line along the junction is worth adding or should be skipped for simplicity.

Instead I'll draw a dark, thin lip line on each side of the snout as a short curved sweep from near the tip, draped onto the snout surface so it hugs the geometry rather than floating above or poking through it.

For the nose, I'm placing a small dark scaled sphere near the end of the snout tip to act as the protruding nose shape, positioning it carefully so it sits right at the tip rather than sunk into the surface.

For eyes, I'm thinking inlaid black ovals with a tiny ivory highlight dot and a carved brow arc, decaled onto the skull surface using a local coordinate anchor with a direction vector and size to control placement and orientation.

Now I'm working out the skull sphere's exact center and scale, then computing where the surface lies at the eye's forward offset so I can place the eyes at the correct symmetric left/right position.

For the ears, I'm placing half-dome shapes near the top of the head with a smaller, darker inset sphere to suggest an incised inner circle, mirrored left and right.

Thinking about cheek texture now too, maybe adding small bump spheres for carved fur ruffs.

For the soapstone look, I want smooth polished dark green-gray stone with incised fur lines, mottled lighter veins, rust-brown iron patches, and a warm waxed highlight on top. Defining stone color palette...

Writing noise band logic...

I'm also thinking about color choice for the polar bear soapstone carving — traditional Inuit soapstone tends toward dark green-grey or black, which would clash with a "white" bear, so I need to decide whether to lean into that darker stone look for authenticity or shift toward a paler grey-cream to keep the bear reading clearly.

I'll settle on a mid-light sage-grey stone with mottled variation, dark incised lines marking fur, black eyes and nose, and ivory inlays for claws and teeth to boost contrast and readability.

I'm also thinking about adding unpolished, rougher darker patches near the base of the feet to suggest raw stone, plus incised chevron-style fur texture decals placed as surface decals across the flanks, shoulders, rump, and back, oriented along the body's natural sweep.

Designing textures for tufts and swirl patterns...

Adding scalloped ruff bands around the neck and chest, then thinking through facial details like incised brow lines and small dark whisker dots stuck onto the snout as tiny flattened spheres. I'm also considering whether to suggest teeth, but leaning toward keeping the mouth closed in the resting pose.

Deciding to add small ivory fang cones peeking below the lip line as a subtle detail, skipping the tongue entirely. Now positioning a shoulder hump as a scaled sphere sitting on the spine joint near the top of the body, working out its exact placement based on the spine curve's height at that point.

Setting up haunch bulges on each hip side using additional scaled spheres to add thigh mass, keeping the same stone material and soap paint treatment consistent across all body parts.

I'll bend both knees the same direction, using a single bend direction for the limb rather than per-joint, matching the docs' convention for passing one direction as a list-of-one.

Chain can take a polyline point array directly, with one joint per span, so I'll build legs, spine, neck, and tail as chains with appropriate roles (leg, spine, neck, tail, head, jaw). I'll set up the hierarchy starting with a root "hips" joint near the spine base, with hind legs parenting to it, then build the spine chain next.

Continuing with the neck chain parented off the spine tip, deriving the head joint from the neck's end position and direction, and setting sweep radii for the neck shape.

Checking proportions: neck radius around 0.28 to match head width, head centered near z=1.14 with skull dimensions roughly y=1.05±0.22, so the thick neck will nicely conceal the join with the head. I'm also considering adding a scalloped fur ruff around the neck using a ring of overlapping flattened spheres.

For the ruff, I'll go with a ring of tapering spikes instead of leaf-shaped blades—about 12 spikes, radius .27, length .16, tilted backward to lean away from the line direction, giving a carved scallop look in soapstone color.

On reflection, a spiky mane looks wrong for a smooth soapstone bear carving—that style reads as sharp fur rather than stone. I'll scrap the spike ring and dorsal ridge idea entirely, letting incised decals handle the fur texture instead, and maybe add just a few small pointed blades at the cheeks for a subtle ruff accent.

Working out the cross product confirms thickness runs along X, so the tufts form thin slabs facing sideways with a flame-shaped outline sweeping backward.

I'm verifying the tuft polygon points form a simple, non-self-intersecting shape with a sharp tip, then planning to stack three tufts at different vertical offsets and scales, with a thinner cheek tuft positioned outside the skull.

Now I'm adding fringe tufts along the back of the front legs at the elbow joint, placing three descending tufts per leg using an outline shape rotated to point down and back, reusing the original tuft curve with an adjusted tip.

Next I'm checking that the new tuft outline doesn't self-intersect, confirming the leg mirroring works since the thickness axis stays symmetric. Then I move on to the tail, sweeping a tapered chain from the rump with a rounded tip.

For the decorative engraving, I'll give each decal stroke a dark teal-gray base with a thin offset ivory highlight beneath it to mimic incised, chalk-filled carving lines.

I'll add a small line of ivory-inlaid discs down the spine (around nine, tiny radius) plus a trio across the forehead, keeping the motif subtle and carving-like rather than overdone. Aiming for a texture count in the 5-12 range overall.

I'm settling on six or seven motifs: eye accents, flank tufts, swirl, chest/neck scallop, chevron leg stripes, and incised brow marks. I also considered adding an artist's mark on the underside like traditional Inuit carvings carry syllabics, but since text glyphs may not render properly in SVG, I'll skip the syllabic signature and instead sketch a simple circular glyph mark using paths.

Now I'm working out placement for decals on the body surface, figuring out how direction and up vectors orient each texture depending on which side of the animal they're applied to, since left and right flanks need mirrored orientation when viewed from outside.

Placing flank tufts symmetrically on both sides with curved surface segments, then adding a shoulder swirl decal positioned slightly higher and forward on the shoulder mass.

I'm reconsidering whether to skip separate shoulder/hip muscle masses since legs already overlap the body enough to read as thigh bulges — I'll just bump the leg-top radius slightly so that bulge is more visible without adding extra geometry.

For surface decoration, I'm placing swirl and spiral decals on the body surface at the haunch and shoulder points, but worrying that the thicker leg sweep geometry there might physically poke above the body and bury the decals, so I may need to adjust leg radius or decal offset to keep them visible.

I need flank tufts placed between the legs on the body, around y=0.95, z=-0.1, avoiding overlap with leg positions, sized moderately. Then for the back decal I'm aiming it upward from a point near the spine's top surface, around y=1.4, dir straight up.

For the chest area, since it's mostly tucked under the neck and skull from the front, I'll angle a scallop decal along the neck's top surface instead, placing it near y=1.38-1.40 where the neck curve meets its radius, oriented upward.

I need to be careful about where the body top actually sits—the spine path interpolation puts it around y=1.42-1.5, with the hump sphere extending to 1.54. Since I'm unsure whether `at` points get projected via nearest-surface or ray-casting, the safer approach is to cast a ray downward from above the surface and use that hit point as my `at` coordinate, doing the same ray-from-outside technique for the side decals.

I'll write a small helper that casts a ray and returns the hit (or null), using `hit.at` as the placement point—since a Hit also sets `dir` to its surface normal automatically, I may not need to specify `dir` separately. For the `up` vector I still want to set it explicitly though, since the normal alone won't guarantee the orientation stays upright—I'll fall back to a different up axis if the hit normal is too close to parallel with my default up vector.

Now I'm figuring out the mirror option: I want to mirror the texture on the +X side so tufts on both flanks sweep the same visual direction when viewed from outside, similar to how the docs example mirrors eye textures. I'm working through the camera orientation at +X looking toward -X to figure out which way "right" points for the viewer, so I can decide if tufts should lean left or right in the source texture.

Next I'm planning other decal placements, like a brow texture with arcs and forehead fur ticks applied to the top of the skull.

I also want a forehead chevron pattern converging into three dark V-shaped incised lines, plus whisker dots on the muzzle rendered as small stick spheres. For the legs I'm adding chevron stripe decals positioned along the lower leg sweep.

Still writing leg sweep logic...

Since the toes are individual spheres, grooves naturally form between them without extra carving, so that part is fine as is. For the eyes, I'm thinking of them as soapstone-carved almond shapes with a dark iris against an ivory sclera, applied as a decal onto the skull surface.

Designing the eye shape and colors...

Adding more color variants...

Still writing shader color blending...

I'm deciding flat colors for the nose, eyes, claws, and inner ear, keeping the mouth area simple without a visible interior, then setting up the builder and bone hierarchy for the soapstone polar bear model.

For the standing pose, I'll keep all four legs slightly apart for a natural stance. I'm bumping the paint texture resolution to 2048 for finer detail given the body's size, then sweeping the spine into a smooth rounded body using a higher side count for that carved soapstone look.

For the body profile, I'm shifting the sweep downward slightly to arch the back and drop the belly, then defining keyframed radius values along the spine so the chest reads deeper and fuller than the rest of the torso.

I'm checking proportions—the belly should bottom out near where the legs attach, and the neck radius needs to taper down from a wider base near the chest to a narrower point near the head, keeping the cheek ruff area visually distinct. I'm shaping the neck path with a gentle downward curve so the head sits low, matching a polar bear's characteristic stance.

Working through head sizing now: the skull and snout dimensions push the total body length to around 3.1 meters, with the head taking up nearly 40% of that—stylized and cute rather than realistic, but acceptable for this design. I'm setting up local coordinate helpers on the head joint to position the jaw bone, defining its joint and aim points relative to the head so it can open and close naturally, then starting the sweep path for the lower jaw geometry.

Writing jaw sweep shape...

I'm checking that the jaw sits mostly inside the skull at the rear so there's no visible gap, and deciding to skip hidden lower canines since they'd be covered by the lips, instead planning visible upper fangs hanging just below the snout tip where it meets the jawline.

To add readability, I'm opening the jaw slightly by rotating its bone a few degrees forward, creating a small gap at the tip, then filling that gap with a dark mouth interior and placing ivory canine cones pointing down from the snout and up from the jaw to show through the opening.

I realize parts need to be built before posing the jaw so they inherit the rotation correctly—otherwise anything attached after posing lands in the wrong frame. I'm positioning the upper fang cones near the snout's bottom edge, orienting them to point downward from their base.

Checking the math, the fang base sits just inside the snout surface while the tip pokes slightly below it, but the closed jaw's top edge would actually cover that protrusion—so opening the jaw by a small angle should expose the tip properly.

Now I'm thinking about the mouth interior itself: should there be a dark capsule shape inside the gap to suggest depth, positioned where the jaw meets the snout? I need to decide whether that interior piece stays hidden when the mouth is closed and only becomes visible once it opens, which affects how I place and scale it relative to the jawbone.

Then I'm moving to the nose: a small dark rounded sphere at the tip of the snout, scaled slightly to match the snout's taper, with high gloss. I'll skip adding separate nostril details and keep the nose simple.

For the eyes, I'm computing their position using the skull's ellipsoid geometry to find where they sit on the surface, placing them small and set wide apart to match a carved-bear look, then setting up a decal ray from that point aimed back toward the head's center axis.

I'm adding small brow ridges above each eye using scaled soap stone spheres, and considering a forehead chevron decal across the top of the skull, before moving on to work out ear placement using similar ellipsoid math at the top of the head.

Cheek tufts positioned at head-left offset with forward .14, extruded backward so tips hang off the skull surface like a ruff, partially embedded where the outline meets the skull. I'm noting the extrude direction is model-back rather than head-aligned, but since the head tilt is slight it shouldn't matter much.

I plan three tufts with different forward/up offsets and scales (1.0, 0.9, 0.75), writing a tuftOutline helper that scales the shape. Next I'm working on fringe tufts at the front-leg elbow, pointing down-back using a TUFT_DOWN orientation, placed relative to the elbow joint where the leg surface curves backward.

Thinking the fin forms thin vertical feathering at the back of the leg, and I'll skip similar fringe for hind legs. Now I'm specifying bones for body-held parts and defining paw geometry, with hind legs using a plantigrade flat sole and slightly larger scale than front paws.

Naming the joints as shoulder/elbow/wrist for front legs and hip/knee/ankle for hind legs, with L/R suffixes marking left as +X. I'm placing small toe spheres along each paw with slight offsets and sizes so they protrude just past the paw tip, plus adding tiny ivory claw cones at each toe.

Each paw now has 5 toes plus 5 claws, giving 40 extra parts across all four paws, which fits within a roughly 250-part budget. I'm double-checking toe sphere scale and vertical placement so they sit flush against the paw surface.

For the spine, I'm planning small bead discs along the body using a sweep-based placement function, stuck onto the dorsal centerline between t=.1 and .95. I need to make sure these beads don't get buried under the hump geometry around the mid-back, so I may need to skip or restrict that range near the hump.

Instead of worrying about sweep coordinates clashing with the hump, I switch to a more robust approach: combine body, hump, and neck into a single surface and shoot downward rays at intervals along z to find hit points for the beads. This way the beads automatically conform to whichever part of the anatomy is highest at that point, including the hump and neck region up to about z=0.85.

Beads will taper slightly in size and orient along the surface normal at each hit point. For the hind legs, I'm thickening the thigh radii to give a haunch-like bulge near the hip joint, and working out the hip joint offset position for the hind leg attachment.

For the front legs, I'm figuring out they should parent to the spine's tip joint rather than a generic point, since the spine's catmull curve with four control points produces three spans plus a tip joint—matching the convention that joint names equal span count plus one. I'm applying the same logic to the neck (two spans, three joints) and tail chains to make sure each gets the right number of named joints.

I'm working out skin weighting: the body uses the spine chain plus hips as root, while the tail and neck get their own separate sweep chains so seams stay hidden under overlapping geometry. The rump cap rides rigidly on the first spine joint, and I'm placing a hump sphere bound to a later spine joint with its own scale and position.

Now I'm recalculating heights -- adjusting the body's radius keyframes and hump placement so the hump actually pokes above the back silhouette instead of getting swallowed by it, settling on a shoulder height around 1.5m which is plausible for a polar bear. I'm also checking that the front legs' segment lengths cover the shoulder-to-ground distance and that enough leg length remains visible below the body's underside rather than being hidden inside it.

Now I'm writing a texture-generation function that scatters small tuft/fur strokes across a grid, computing each stroke's position, lean, and curve as a quadratic path with a chalky highlight layer plus a dark ink outline layer, tuning stroke widths and column spacing so the fur marks render at a reasonable pixel size without bleeding past the viewBox edges.

For the swirl texture, I'm computing a spiral path by sampling points along an increasing angle and radius, then drawing two of these spirals offset 180 degrees apart to form a double-arm spiral pattern with a chalky underline layer, scaling the radius range to fit the 100x100 viewBox.

For scallop, I'm drawing rows of small semicircular arcs to create a fish-scale pattern, alternating offsets across five rows for use on the neck and chest. For chevron legs, I'm generating horizontal zigzag polylines across five bands spanning the width for a leg pattern.

For the forehead marking, I'm sketching V-shaped chevron ticks at a few vertical positions with a brow arc above. For the sign glyph, I'm drawing simple symbol shapes—a triangle, a curved loop, and a dot—inside a circular outline.

Deciding placement for the decal: thicker dark strokes at small scale, positioned on the left hind leg thigh's outer side, below the swirl marking.

Now I'm designing the eye SVG — an almond-shaped incised outline with a dark fill and thin chalky stroke border, plus an ivory highlight ellipse and a smaller secondary dot to give it depth, with an upper lid arc above.

Placing whisker dots using nearest-surface lookups on the snout, arranged in rows of three on each side with small sphere geometry markers.

Then I plan the mouth line as a draped path along the snout's lower side, curving from the cheek area to a point near the nose tip, lifted slightly off the surface to avoid clipping.

Now I'm starting to write the implementation code for the model's geometry and surface decorations.

Still defining the keyframe interpolation helper, then starting the main build function for the polar bear rig with a hip joint as the spine root.

I'm chaining the spine joints along a catmull-rom path from hips to chest, then sweeping a body profile along that spine with varying radii to shape the torso.

Now I'm working out the limb loop, iterating over left/right sides and setting up front leg points while avoiding strict TypeScript typing by using `any`-ish return types for the sweep results.

Still writing limb chains...

Reducing hind leg lengths to .38/.38 gives a more moderate knee offset of .16, which I'll use for the chain. I'm naming the hip, knee, and ankle joints for the hind leg, then writing a helper function that casts a ray against a target surface to find a hit point and places a decal there with the given texture and size.

To avoid recomputing surfaces repeatedly, I'll cache them in a map keyed by target so poses only re-read when needed. Now I'm starting to lay out the actual decals, beginning with tufts on the body flank, mirrored left and right.

For the back, I'm placing a tuft with a dorsal orientation, then second-guessing whether a chevron-based herringbone pattern along the spine would read better than a single leaning tuft, considering a forehead-style V-chevron oriented along the back direction instead.

Working out thigh swirl and lower leg chevron placements...

Adding the forehead decal orientation, then setting up spine beads and face part declarations with the jaw pose and color constants. Now I'm defining the head joint relative to the neck's end point, and starting on the jaw joint parameters.

Adding snout taper and jaw sweep...

Checking the nose position relative to the snout cap, confirming it sits slightly above and forward correctly. I'm positioning the mouth, jaw rotation pivot, and now setting up cheek tufts with extruded outlines in the head region.

Working through the tuft geometry, I realize the tuft root sits inside the skull surface at that forward position since the skull's side boundary extends further out than the tuft's starting point -- so only the backward-extending part of the tuft would actually protrude beyond the skull where it narrows.

Checking a thicker, farther-out variant confirms the tufts emerge properly as slabs poking outside the skull, fading in gradually like a ruff collar. Now I'm shifting to the ear's inner geometry, positioning a small flattened sphere offset slightly from the ear position along a normalized direction vector to create the inner ear detail.

I'm also laying out beads along the spine, using a surface combining the body, hump, and neck sections, adjusting the z-range so the rump cap at the bottom isn't too flattened by the ray intersection.

Now I'm checking that the back decals don't collide with the beads since both sit slightly above the surface, then starting to write a helper function for placing the paws.

Adding toe spheres and claw positioning...

Counting joints across legs totals a reasonable number, and I'm double-checking contact points, root pose height, and floor collision for paws and tail. I'm adding type-safety checks for nullable tips and hits, then moving on to writing the SVG helper functions for details like tufts.

Writing tuft generator...

Drawing chevron shapes...

I'm checking whether the snout geometry overlaps the eye placement on the skull surface, since the snout's sweep at that forward position nearly covers where the eye sits. I'm adjusting the eye position further forward and outward to keep it clear of the snout surface.

I'm now also considering whether to add a separate brow ridge shape or leave the brow detail to the texture decal, working out where a small ridge sphere would sit relative to the skull surface curvature.

Defining the outline point type and tuft helper function...
